unit.title: Prepare and cook meat and seafood

summary: This unit teaches you to receive, store, prepare and cook meat and seafood safely: beef, goat, pork and oxtail, fish, shrimp and saltfish. You will learn how to judge freshness, choose the cooking method to match the cut, and cook Jamaican favourites such as curry goat, stewed oxtail, jerk pork, escovitch fish, steamed fish, run down and pepper shrimp. You will also learn the food safety rules, how to hold, cool, store and reheat, and how to serve guests with allergies.

blocks.p: Meat and seafood are the most expensive items on most menus and the ones that guests remember. Cooked well, curry goat or escovitch fish is the best dish of a guest's holiday. Cooked badly, or handled carelessly, it can make people seriously ill. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

Raw meat, poultry and fish carry bacteria. Some fish carry natural toxins that cooking does not destroy. Shellfish and fish are among the foods that cause the most dangerous allergic reactions. So this unit is about **safety, hygiene and judgement**, as much as about cooking skill.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's training kitchen. In the practical tasks you cook curry goat and grilled pork, clean and fry whole fish for escovitch fish, and prepare pepper shrimp. The assessor watches your safety, hygiene, timing, tasting and clean-up as well as the finished plate.

blocks.h: Hygiene rules for meat and seafood

ul: **Wash your hands** before you start, after touching raw meat or fish, waste, your face or the toilet, and between jobs.

Use **colour-coded boards**, knives and tongs: a common code is red for raw meat, blue for raw fish and seafood, yellow for cooked meat, green for salad and fruit, brown for root vegetables. Your Centre's code decides.
Never use the same board, knife or tongs for raw and cooked food without washing and sanitising them first.
Keep raw meat and fish **below** cooked and ready-to-eat foods in the fridge, covered, so that the juices cannot drip.
Do not wash raw meat or poultry under the tap; splashes spread bacteria around the sink. Cooking kills the germs.
Clean as you go. Clear the waste, wash and sanitise the bench and tools after raw food before you start the next job.
Cover cuts with a blue plaster and a glove, and do not come to work with vomiting or diarrhoea.
Hold a Food Handler's Permit from the health department, as the law in Jamaica requires for food handlers.

blocks.p: **Fish**, **crustaceans** (shrimp, lobster, crab) and **molluscs** (conch, oysters, mussels) are among the allergens that guests must be told about, together with eggs, milk, nuts, peanuts, soya, wheat (gluten), celery, mustard and sesame.

ul: **Cross-contact** happens when a trace of an allergen gets into food that does not contain it, for example through shared oil, a shared pot or board, or a spoon. Even a trace can cause a severe reaction.
When an order has an allergy: tell the chef, check every recipe and label, use clean equipment and fresh oil, and make sure the plate reaches the right guest.
Never guess, never pick the allergen out of the dish, and never say 'it should be all right'.
If a guest has a reaction (swelling, difficulty breathing, a rash, vomiting), call for help at once. In Jamaica, call 110 for an ambulance.
Check the **temperature**: chilled meat and fish should arrive at 5 °C or below, and frozen food at -18 °C or below and hard. Use a clean probe.
Check the **packaging**, the **date**, and the supplier's details. Reject torn, wet, leaking or dirty packs.
Check the **quality** (see the tables below). Reject anything that does not pass and report it to your supervisor.
Check the **quantity** against the order.
Record the temperature and any problem, and put the food away quickly. Do not leave it on the loading bay in the sun.

head: Food
Fresh: accept
Not fresh: reject
rows: Bright, natural colour (beef bright red, pork pale pink); firm, springy, slightly moist; fresh smell.
Grey, green or brown patches; slimy, sticky or dry surface; sour or strong smell.
Bright, clear, bulging eyes; red or pink gills; shiny, firm skin with scales in place; firm flesh that springs back; fresh sea smell; no belly burst.
Dull, sunken eyes; brown or grey gills; dull, slimy skin; soft flesh that stays dented; strong ammonia or 'fishy' smell.
Moist, translucent, firm, with no browning at the edges; fresh smell.
Dry, gaping, browned or slimy flesh; sour smell.
Firm, shiny, translucent shell; mild sea smell; heads attached firmly.
Soft, slimy shells; black spots; ammonia smell; heads that fall off.
Frozen hard, packaging whole, no ice crystals or freezer burn.
Soft or thawed patches; large ice crystals; dry, white freezer burn; torn pack.

head: Item
Storage rule
rows: Covered, labelled and dated, at **5 °C or below**, on the **bottom shelf** so that juices cannot drip onto other food. Raw fish on ice or in a covered tray, and used first. Check the fridge temperature every day and write it on the temperature log.
Covered, labelled and dated, above raw meat.
At **-18 °C or below**, labelled with the date. First in, first out. Do not refreeze food that has fully thawed.
In a cool, dry, covered place, or in the fridge. Soak and cook before use.
Covered and labelled in the fridge, never on the counter.
Cool, dry store; check dates and cans.

blocks.note: Raw meat juices dripping onto food on a lower shelf is a common way for germs to spread. Keep raw meat on the bottom shelf, in a deep tray with a lid.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Best:** in the fridge, on the bottom shelf, in a covered tray. Large items such as a goat shoulder or a whole fish can take a day or two.
**Quick method for fish fillets, shrimp or small items to be cooked at once:** sealed in a watertight bag under cold running water, until thawed.
**Never** thaw meat or fish on the counter, near the stove, in warm water or in the sun. The outside warms in the danger zone while the inside is still frozen.
Cook soon after thawing, and never refreeze it unless it has been cooked first.
Pat thawed meat or fish dry with kitchen paper before cooking: it browns and fries better, and spits less.

head: Risk
What it is
What you do
rows: In fish such as tuna, mackerel, mahi-mahi and kingfish, bacteria turn a natural chemical into histamine if the fish gets warm. Histamine is not destroyed by cooking. It causes a flushed face, headache and rash soon after eating.
Buy only fish that has been kept cold all the way from the boat. Keep it on ice at the kitchen; cook it soon.
A natural toxin in some large reef fish (for example barracuda), which builds up in fish that eat smaller reef fish. Cooking does not destroy it. It causes stomach illness and nerve symptoms.
Buy large reef fish only from a trusted supplier who follows local advice.
Can carry germs that cause illness; spoil quickly; strong allergen.
Buy from licensed suppliers, keep cold, cook until firm and opaque, tell guests about the allergen.

blocks.note: Lobster and conch fishing in Jamaica have closed seasons and rules to protect the stocks. Buy only from licensed suppliers, who follow the law. Ask your instructor for the current rules.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Meat: cuts, tenderness and choosing the method

blocks.p: Meat is made of muscle fibres held together by **connective tissue** (the main part is a protein called **collagen**) and some fat. A muscle that works hard in the animal's life, such as the leg, shoulder, tail, neck and foot, has a lot of collagen and is tough. A muscle that does little work, such as the loin or fillet along the back, has little collagen and is tender.

ul: **Quick, dry heat** (grilling, frying, roasting) cooks tender cuts quickly. On a tough cut, it leaves the meat chewy, because the collagen stays hard.

**Long, slow, moist heat** (stewing, braising, boiling) turns collagen into soft **gelatine**, which makes the meat tender and the sauce rich. That is why oxtail, cow foot, shin and goat are cooked for a long time.
Older animals have tougher meat; goat and mutton need longer cooking than kid or lamb.
**Marbling**: thin lines of fat inside the muscle melt as it cooks and keep the meat juicy.

head: Meat
Cuts and uses
Usual method
rows: Tender cuts: grill, fry or roast. Tough cuts: stew, braise or boil. Mince: cook right through.
Leg, shoulder, ribs and neck, usually chopped with the bone, for curry goat
Head and tripe for mannish water
Long, slow, moist cooking: curry, stew or braise.
Cook through; jerk pork is cooked slowly over pimento wood or charcoal, or in an oven.
Often salted and boiled; handle with care and cook well.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, the word 'mutton' often means goat meat. A butcher will tell you which it is. In classical cookery, mutton is the meat of an older sheep, and goat is a different animal.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Method
Heat
Suits
Example
rows: Tender cuts: steaks, chops, fish steaks
Tender, small or coated pieces, fish
Moist, slow, covered, in a little liquid
Salted meat, cow foot, soup bones
Oxtail and cow foot in about an hour

head: Food
Core temperature (typical)
Notes
rows: Cook right through. Mincing mixes surface bacteria all through the meat.
Pork, goat, and cut-up or rolled meat
As the guest orders: rare, medium or well done
Only the outside is contaminated, and searing kills the germs there. This applies to a whole cut only, never to mince or rolled meat.
About 63 °C, or until the flesh is opaque and flakes

blocks.note: A guest who asks for a steak rare or medium-rare is choosing a risk for himself. The kitchen can serve it to order from a whole, fresh cut, but must warn children, the elderly, pregnant women and anyone ill, and cook it fully for them.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Wash your hands; set up the board (red, on a damp cloth) and a sharp knife
Bring only what you need from the fridge, and keep the rest cold
Trim excess fat, gristle and the tough silver skin (the thin, shiny membrane on beef and pork fillet)
Cut to even portions or pieces, as the recipe says
Weigh the portions
Return the meat to the fridge, covered, until it is seasoned or cooked
Wash and sanitise the board, knife and area; wash your hands

ul: Cut across the grain (the direction of the muscle fibres) to shorten the fibres, so that cooked meat is easier to chew. Roast beef is carved across the grain.
To cut goat or oxtail with bone, use a cleaver on a heavy board, with the board on a damp cloth. Hold the meat away from the blade and chop firmly in one stroke.
Weigh the portions so that every plate is the same and the costs are right.
Keep trimmings and clean bones for stock; throw away anything that is spoiled.

blocks.p: A **marinade** or seasoning rub adds flavour and, if it has acid (lime juice, vinegar) or an enzyme (pawpaw), helps soften the outside of the meat. Jamaican seasoning includes salt, black pepper, garlic, thyme, scallion, onion, pimento (allspice), Scotch bonnet pepper, ginger, curry powder, browning and soy sauce.

ul: Season the meat well, and rub the seasoning in; score thick pieces so it can get in.
Marinate **covered and labelled, in the fridge**, never on the counter. Many meats are marinated overnight.
Do not reuse marinade that has touched raw meat as a sauce unless it is boiled first, or make fresh sauce. The safest way is to throw it away.
Wear gloves for Scotch bonnet pepper.
**Slow, moist cooking** is the most reliable way to tenderise tough cuts.
**Pounding** with a meat mallet breaks the fibres of thin steaks and cutlets.
**Marinating** with acid or with pawpaw (papaya) for a short time softens the surface. Too long makes the meat mushy.
**Pressure cooking** softens tough cuts fast.

blocks.note: Pawpaw (papaya) contains an enzyme called papain, which breaks down protein. A little in the seasoning, or wrapping meat in the leaves, softens it. Too much, or too long, turns the meat to mush.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Pat the seasoned meat dry with kitchen paper
Heat oil in a heavy pot; brown the meat in batches, laying pieces away from you
Take out the meat; soften onion, garlic, pepper, tomato and herbs in the pot
Return the meat; add stock or water just to cover (or less for a thick gravy)
Bring to the boil, turn down, cover and **simmer gently** until tender
Add vegetables and provisions near the end, so they do not fall apart
Skim fat, taste with a clean spoon, adjust the seasoning, and thicken if needed
Serve hot on a warm plate

ul: **Why brown the meat first?** Browning adds colour and a deeper, roasted flavour. Do not crowd the pot, or the meat will steam and go grey.
**Why simmer, not boil hard?** Hard boiling makes the meat tough and stringy; the liquid should barely bubble.
**Why a lid?** It holds in heat and moisture. Check the liquid, and add a little hot water if it dries.

flow: Cut the goat into even pieces on the bone; trim the fat; season with curry powder, salt, pepper, garlic, thyme, scallion, onion and pimento; marinate covered in the fridge, best overnight
Heat oil in a heavy pot; fry some curry powder for a minute or two (this is called 'burning the curry' and brings out the flavour); do not let it burn black
Add the goat and brown it, stirring
Add water or stock, a whole unburst Scotch bonnet and thyme; cover and simmer
Cook for about 1½ to 2½ hours until tender (30 to 45 minutes in a pressure cooker, as the maker says)
Add potato towards the end, and cook until soft; it thickens the gravy
Remove the pepper; taste with a clean spoon; serve hot with rice and peas or white rice

ul: Cut the oxtail across the joints. Season well, brown it and simmer it with onions, thyme, scallion, pimento and a little browning.
Cook slowly for about 2½ to 3½ hours (about 45 to 60 minutes in a pressure cooker), until the meat nearly falls off the bone. The collagen has turned to gelatine.
Add **butter beans** (tinned, or dried that have been soaked and boiled hard first) for the last 30 minutes, and cook until the gravy is thick. Skim off the extra fat.

blocks.p: **Jerk** is a Jamaican way of seasoning and slow-cooking meat, from the Maroon tradition. The meat is rubbed with jerk seasoning (Scotch bonnet pepper, pimento (allspice), scallion, thyme, garlic, ginger, salt, pepper and a little vinegar or sugar), marinated, and cooked slowly over pimento wood or charcoal, or in an oven.

flow: Make the jerk seasoning; wear gloves for the peppers
Cut the pork into pieces, score the thick parts and rub the seasoning in
Marinate covered and labelled in the fridge, overnight if possible
Cook slowly over a moderate fire (or in an oven), turning often, so that it browns without burning
Check the core temperature at the thickest part with a clean probe: about 74 °C and no pink juices
Rest, then chop or slice, and serve hot with festival, bammy or hard-dough bread

blocks.note: Use a jerk pan or charcoal grill outdoors only, away from doors and windows and anything that can burn. Never use petrol to light it, never leave it alone, and never throw water on the coals. Charcoal gives off carbon monoxide, which is a deadly gas that you cannot smell.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Grilling and frying steaks and chops

ul: Take the meat from the fridge a little before cooking. Pat it dry and season it.
Heat the grill or pan until very hot, so that the meat browns quickly on the outside.
Turn the meat once or twice with tongs, not a fork (a fork lets the juices out).
Check the core temperature with a clean probe, or by feel and the juices.
**Rest** the meat for a few minutes on a warm plate: the juices settle back in and do not run out when you cut it.
Season, put in a roasting tray (on a trivet of vegetables if you like), and roast in a hot oven to brown it, then lower the heat.
Check the core temperature with a clean probe in the thickest part, not touching bone.
Rest for 15 to 30 minutes, covered loosely, then **carve across the grain** with a sharp carving knife.
Use the juices in the tray to make gravy.
Follow the maker's instructions. Check the seal, the valve and the vent before use.
Never fill it above the maximum mark (two-thirds for most food, half for beans and foods that foam).
Lock the lid correctly. Turn the heat down when pressure is reached. Never leave it alone.
Let the pressure fall fully before opening, as the maker says. Never force the lid. Open the lid away from your face.
Clean the seal, valve and lid after use.

head: Type
Examples
Notes
rows: Snapper, parrotfish, grouper, jack, kingfish, mackerel
Cooked whole, in steaks or as two fillets.
Four fillets; less common in Jamaica.
Rich flavour; spoil faster; keep very cold.
Saltfish (salted cod), pickled mackerel, smoked herring
Must be soaked or boiled to remove the salt.

flow: Set up a blue board on a damp cloth; have a scaler, a sharp knife, scissors and a waste bowl
Scale the fish from the **tail towards the head**, on both sides, under cold running water if you can
Trim off the fins with scissors, taking care with the spines
Cut open the belly from the vent to the head; take out the guts
Remove the **gills**; they spoil quickly and taste bitter
Wash the cavity well and remove the dark blood line along the backbone
Pat dry; score the sides with 2 or 3 diagonal cuts so the seasoning gets in and the fish cooks evenly
Keep it covered and chilled until you cook it; wash and sanitise the area afterwards

ul: A round fish gives **two fillets**, one from each side.
Use a thin, flexible filleting knife. Cut behind the head down to the backbone, then run the blade along the backbone, over the rib bones, to the tail, keeping it close to the bone.
Turn the fish over and repeat. Check the fillet for pin bones and remove them with tweezers.
Skin if needed: lay the fillet skin-side down, cut a little at the tail end and, holding the skin, slide the knife along it.
Keep the bones and heads for fish stock; rinse out the gills first.
Keep raw shrimp on ice or at 5 °C or below until you cook them.
**Peel**: pull off the legs and head, and then the shell. You can leave the tail on.
**Devein**: with the point of a knife, cut a shallow line along the back and lift out the dark thread (the gut). It can be gritty.
Rinse, drain and pat dry. Use a blue board and wash your hands after.
Cook shrimp **briefly** until they turn pink and firm and opaque. Overcooking makes them tough and rubbery.

flow: Rinse the saltfish under cold water
Soak in cold water for several hours, changing the water, or boil for 10 to 20 minutes, drain and repeat if still too salty
Taste a small piece to check the saltiness
Remove the skin and every bone: bones are a choking hazard
Flake the fish with your fingers
Use at once, or cover, label and chill

head: Method
How
Notes
rows: Season; pat dry; shallow or deep fry in hot oil, at about 170 to 180 °C, until golden and cooked through
Lay the fish into the oil away from your body; do not crowd the pan; turn once; drain on paper.
Season; cook covered with okra, carrot, cho cho and a little water until the flesh flakes
Gentle and healthy; keeps the fish moist.
Fish, such as salted or fresh mackerel, simmered in coconut milk with onion, tomato, thyme and pepper until the milk cooks down to a thick sauce
Serve with dumplings, green banana or breadfruit.
Season; grill or roast over heat or in the oven; turn once
Oil the grill; do not move the fish until it releases.
Cook gently in stock or court bouillon
Fish tea; do not boil hard.
Fried fish simmered in a brown gravy

flow: Clean, score and season the fish with salt, black pepper and a little lime juice; pat dry
Fry in hot oil until golden and the flesh flakes; drain on paper
Slice onion, carrot, sweet pepper, cho cho and Scotch bonnet in thin strips (gloves for the pepper)
Boil vinegar, water, pimento berries, salt and pepper for a few minutes; add the vegetables for 1 to 2 minutes only, so they stay a little crisp
Pour the hot pickle over the fried fish
Serve with bammy or festival; chill leftovers quickly and label them

ul: Peel and devein the shrimp or boil them in the shell; boil in water with pepper, salt, garlic, thyme and pimento until pink and firm, about 3 to 5 minutes.
Drain, then toss in or serve with hot pepper sauce, garlic and scallion.
Serve hot, or chill fast and serve cold the same day.
Wear gloves for the peppers, and tell guests that shrimp is a shellfish and may be hot.

blocks.note: Middle Quarters in St. Elizabeth is famous for pepper shrimp, sold by roadside vendors. In a kitchen, the same rules apply: shrimp from a licensed supplier, kept cold, cooked until firm and pink, and kept hot or chilled fast.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: How to tell when fish is cooked

ul: The flesh turns **opaque** (no longer see-through) and flakes easily when pressed with a fork at the thickest part.
The core temperature is about 63 °C, or as your Centre's plan says.
The flesh comes away from the bone.
Shrimp turn pink and firm, and curl into a loose C-shape (a tight ring means overcooked).
**Taste with a clean spoon every time**, and put the used spoon in the wash-up. Never put a used spoon back in the pot.
Adjust salt, pepper, acid (lime juice), heat and thickness. Salted meats and stock cubes add salt.
Remove the whole Scotch bonnet before serving; take out thyme stalks, bay leaves and bones if the recipe says.
Skim the fat from stews and gravies.
Serve hot food on **warm** plates and cold food on cold plates.
Weigh portions so that each plate is the same and costs are right.
Put the main item where the guest sees it first; keep gravy off the rim; wipe the rim clean; do not overfill.
Garnish simply: a sprig of thyme, a slice of lime, or the escovitch pickle on the fish.
Serve with the usual accompaniments: rice and peas, bammy, festival, boiled green banana, breadfruit or vegetables.

head: Step
Rule
rows: Keep food at about 63 °C or above, in a bain-marie or hot cupboard; check with a clean probe. Do not use hot-holding to reheat.

Divide large pots into shallow trays; chill in an ice bath or blast chiller; do not leave a pot to cool on the stove. Cool from hot to about 21 °C within 2 hours and then to 5 °C within a further 4 hours (a common guide).
Cover, label and date; keep at 5 °C or below, below ready-to-eat foods and above raw.
Quickly, to about 74 °C in the centre, checked with a probe and recorded. Reheat **once only**; throw away what is left.
Keep hot food hot (63 °C or above), cold food cold (5 °C or below), and throw away what has stood out for too long. Do not top up old food with new food.

ul: Weigh the portions and follow the standard recipe.
Use the whole animal or fish: bones and heads for stock; trimmings for sauces and soups.

A recipe is scaled by dividing the amount by the number of portions it makes and multiplying by the number you need. For example, 2 kg of goat for 10 portions is 0.2 kg per portion, so for 25 portions you need 0.2 × 25 = 5 kg.
Record waste so that your supervisor can see where money is lost.
Clear the waste into the right bins, and wipe up fish water and meat juice.
Wash, rinse and sanitise boards, knives, tongs, pots and surfaces; dry them.
Clean the grill, the jerk pan and the fryer area; let used oil cool and strain it; store or dispose of it as your Centre says.
Wash and clean the pressure cooker seal, valve and lid.
Wash your hands; record temperatures on the temperature log.

terms: Collagen
The connective tissue in meat; turns to gelatine in long, slow, moist cooking.
Gelatine
The soft jelly that collagen becomes; it makes stews rich and meat tender.
Marbling
Thin lines of fat inside meat that keep it juicy.
Silver skin
The thin, tough, shiny membrane trimmed from meat such as beef fillet.
Grain
The direction in which the muscle fibres run; carve across it.
Marinade
A seasoned liquid or rub in which food is soaked for flavour.
Braising
Slow cooking in a covered pot with a little liquid.
Stewing
Slow cooking of small pieces in a sauce.
Searing
Browning the outside of meat quickly in a very hot pan or grill.
Resting
Leaving cooked meat for a few minutes so that the juices settle.
Core temperature
The temperature in the middle of the thickest part of the food.
Jerk
A Jamaican way of seasoning and slow-cooking meat over pimento wood or charcoal.
Escovitch
Fried fish topped with a hot, spiced vinegar pickle of onion, carrot and pepper.
Run down
Fish simmered in coconut milk until it cooks down to a thick sauce.
Saltfish
Dried, salted fish, used in ackee and saltfish.
Fillet
A piece of fish or meat cut away from the bone.
Deveining
Taking out the dark gut from the back of a shrimp.
Opaque
Not see-through; fish flesh turns opaque when cooked.
Histamine
A chemical that forms in fish kept warm; it causes illness and is not destroyed by cooking.
Ciguatera
A natural toxin in some large reef fish; it is not destroyed by cooking.
Cross-contact
The passing of a trace of an allergen into food that should not contain it.
Cross-contamination
The passing of germs from raw to ready-to-eat food.
Danger zone
The temperature range, about 5 °C to 63 °C, in which bacteria grow fastest.
FIFO
First in, first out: use the oldest stock first.

c1.title: A delivery to a hotel kitchen in Falmouth
c1.text: A supplier delivers to a hotel kitchen in Falmouth at 11 a.m. in an open pickup. The snapper is packed with only a little ice, and some of the fish have sunken eyes and brown gills. A box of raw shrimp feels soft and smells of ammonia. A carton of goat is partly soft, with ice crystals, and a pack of beef mince reads 11 °C on the probe. Trainee Andre is told to sign for it all quickly, because the loading bay is needed.

c2.title: Escovitch fish at a beach restaurant in Hellshire
c2.text: At a beach restaurant at Hellshire, trainee Shanique cleans and fries snapper for the lunch rush. She scrapes the scales from the head towards the tail, leaves the gills in, and puts the fish straight from the bowl, wet, into very hot oil. The oil spits. She then picks up the Scotch bonnet peppers for the pickle with bare hands and rubs her eye. A customer has said that she cannot eat shellfish, and a pan of pepper shrimp was fried in the same oil an hour ago.

c3.title: Oxtail and curry goat for Sunday dinner in Mandeville
c3.text: A restaurant in Mandeville is cooking stewed oxtail and curry goat for Sunday dinner. Trainee Dwight puts the oxtail in the pot with water and cooks it on a hard boil for 30 minutes, and finds it tough and chewy. He also plans to use the pressure cooker for the goat, filling it to the top, and to open it at once. After service there are 8 litres of oxtail stew left in a deep pot, which he leaves on the stove to cool.

c4.title: A jerk centre in Boston Bay, Portland
c4.text: At a jerk centre in Boston Bay, Portland, trainee Kareem is helping to cook pork over pimento wood. The pieces were seasoned that morning and left on the table in the sun. He moves them with the same tongs that he used for the raw pork, and chops them on the same board. The outside is black and the inside of the thickest piece looks pink. His chef asks him to check it with a probe.

c5.title: Saltfish and run down at a guesthouse in St. Ann's Bay
c5.text: A guesthouse in St. Ann's Bay has ordered saltfish and mackerel for breakfast. Trainee Natalee puts the saltfish in a pan, rinses it once and fries it with onion and tomatoes for an ackee dish. The dish is far too salty, and a guest complains of a small bone. Later she is told to make run down using mackerel, coconut milk, onion, tomato and thyme.

questions.q: What should Andre do about the delivery before he signs for it?
o: Sign for everything now and sort out any problems after the lunch rush
Check the temperature, quality and dates, and reject what fails
Refuse only the beef mince, as the rest is probably safe once it is cooked
Put the box of shrimp on top of the ice and accept it with the rest
questions.why: Receiving is a food safety check. Unacceptable items must be rejected and reported, and signing first would mean the kitchen has accepted them.

questions.q: What does the soft, ammonia-smelling box of shrimp tell you?
o: It is only the sea salt that gives the smell and the soft feel
It is normal for shrimp that have been frozen at some time
It is stale and has started to spoil, so it must be rejected
It can be used if the shrimp are cooked until very well done
questions.why: Fresh shrimp are firm and shiny with a mild sea smell. A soft, slimy shell and an ammonia smell show that they are spoiling, and cooking will not make them safe.

questions.q: What is the reading of 11 °C on the beef mince?
o: Fine, because mince is cooked right through later
Too warm, because chilled meat should arrive at 5 °C or below
Fine, as long as it was packed in a sealed bag
Fine, because mince is allowed to arrive at up to 12 °C
questions.why: Chilled meat should be at 5 °C or below on arrival. At 11 °C, bacteria are growing, and mince, which has surface bacteria mixed all through, is the most risky.

questions.q: Which sign of freshness is Andre looking for on the snapper that these fish do NOT have?
o: A strong smell that shows the fish is well flavoured
Dull, flat eyes and gills that are brown
Firm flesh, bright clear eyes and red or pink gills
Slimy skin and flesh that stays dented when pressed
questions.why: A fresh fish has bright, clear eyes, red or pink gills, shiny skin and firm flesh. Sunken eyes and brown gills show that it is old.

questions.q: Shanique scraped the scales from head to tail. What is the right way to scale a fish?
o: From the head towards the tail, along the lie of the scales
From the tail up towards the head, against the lie of the scales
In small circles, working from the belly up to the back
From the belly to the back, along the whole of the side
questions.why: Scales overlap towards the tail, so scraping from tail to head lifts them off cleanly. Working with the scales leaves many behind.

questions.q: What is the main risk of putting the wet fish straight into very hot oil?
o: The fish will absorb too much salt from the oil
The oil will cool down so much that the fish turns grey
The wet skin will always stick to the bottom of the pan
The water makes the oil spit and splash, and can burn her
questions.why: Water and hot oil react violently and spit. Pat the fish dry first, and lay it into the oil away from your body.

questions.q: Shanique rubbed her eye after cutting Scotch bonnet. What is the best advice?
o: Rinse the eye gently with plenty of clean, cool water and tell the supervisor
Rub the eye with a cloth soaked in vinegar and carry on
Put a drop of cooking oil in the eye, to coat the burning
Carry on, as the burning will stop within a few minutes
questions.why: Pepper oil burns the eye. Rinse it gently with clean, cool water for several minutes, and report it. Gloves would have prevented it.

questions.q: What must the kitchen do for the guest who cannot eat shellfish?
o: Fry her fish in the same oil, since the shrimp pieces have been taken out
Tell her that the fish will taste of the shrimp and let her decide
Use clean equipment and fresh oil, and tell the chef at once
Fry her fish on a clean board, then turn up the heat to kill any traces
questions.why: A trace of shellfish from shared oil can cause a severe reaction, and heat does not remove the allergen. The chef must know, and clean equipment and fresh oil must be used.

questions.q: Why was Dwight's oxtail tough after 30 minutes of hard boiling?
o: A cut with a lot of collagen needs long, slow, moist cooking to soften
The oxtail was too fresh, so it will soften only after it has been frozen
Hard boiling toughens meat because it removes all of its fat
Oxtail should always be cooked in a dry oven to make it soft
questions.why: Oxtail is full of collagen, which turns to soft gelatine only with long, slow cooking at a simmer. Fast boiling toughens the fibres.

questions.q: Dwight fills the pressure cooker to the top and wants to open it at once. What is the right action?
o: Fill it to two-thirds at most, and open it once the pressure has fallen fully
Fill it to the top, then release the steam quickly with a spoon
Leave it half open to let the steam out as the meat cooks
Fill it as he plans, then run cold water over it at once
questions.why: Overfilling can block the valve, and opening too early causes a violent steam release. Follow the maker's instructions and wait until the pressure has fallen.

questions.q: What should Dwight do with the 8 litres of oxtail stew left in the deep pot?
o: Leave it on the stove overnight and put it in the fridge in the morning
Put the whole hot pot on the bottom shelf of the fridge
Chill it fast in shallow trays, then cover, label and date it
Keep it warm in the oven overnight, so it is ready to serve for lunch
questions.why: A big pot of hot stew cools slowly and stays in the danger zone. Shallow trays and an ice bath bring it down fast, and then it is covered, labelled and dated.

questions.q: The stew is reheated for the next day's lunch. How should it be done?
o: Warm it gently in the bain-marie until it feels hot to the touch
Reheat it quickly to about 74 °C in the centre, and do this once only
Reheat it, and then cool and reheat it again if there is any left
Bring it to a warm 50 °C so that the gravy does not catch
questions.why: Reheat quickly to about 74 °C in the centre, checked with a probe, once only. A bain-marie is for holding, not reheating, and each reheat gives bacteria another chance.

questions.q: Where should Kareem have kept the seasoned pork until cooking?
o: On a table in the shade, covered with a clean cloth
In a covered, labelled container in the fridge
In a pan of cold water on the table, so it stays cool
On a rack above the fire so it starts to warm through
questions.why: Seasoned raw meat must stay at 5 °C or below. In the sun, in the danger zone, bacteria grow fast.

questions.q: What is wrong with using the same tongs and board for the raw and cooked pork?
o: Raw pork makes the tongs too slippery to hold the cooked pieces
The cooked pork would pick up germs from the raw pork
The cooked pork would lose its colour and flavour
The board would blunt the knife as it chops the bones
questions.why: Germs on the raw pork pass to the cooked meat by the tongs and board, which is cross-contamination. Use separate, clean tongs and boards for raw and cooked, or wash and sanitise them between.

questions.q: The jerk is black outside and pink inside. What does this show?
o: It is cooked, because a black outside means the heat has gone through
It is raw inside and needs gentler heat, checked with a probe
It is fine, because pork is safe to serve pink when well seasoned
It is ready, because the pink colour is from the pimento wood smoke
questions.why: A fierce fire burns the outside before the inside is cooked. Move it to a gentler heat and cook until the thickest part is about 74 °C, checked with a clean probe.

questions.q: Why was Natalee's saltfish dish too salty?
o: The saltfish was not soaked or boiled and the water changed to take out the salt
She added too much tomato, which makes saltfish taste of salt
She fried the saltfish for too long, which draws salt out of it
The onion was cooked first, and this brings out more salt
questions.why: Saltfish is preserved in salt and must be soaked in cold water (changed several times) or boiled and drained, then tasted, before it is cooked in a dish.

questions.q: How could the bone have been avoided?
o: By frying the saltfish until the bones go soft and crisp
By adding more liquid to dissolve the bones while it cooks
By flaking the fish and taking out the skin and every bone
By chopping the saltfish small so the bones cannot be felt
questions.why: Skin and bones should be removed after soaking, while flaking the fish. Bones are a choking hazard and a common complaint.

questions.q: What does 'run down' mean for the mackerel?
o: Fried and then served in a vinegar pickle
Steamed with okra and a little water
Grilled over pimento wood and chopped
Simmered in coconut milk until the milk cooks down to a thick sauce
questions.why: Run down is fish simmered in coconut milk with onion, tomato, thyme and pepper until the milk cooks down into a thick sauce. Escovitch is pickled fried fish, and steamed fish is cooked with okra.

questions.q: A cook cuts a rested roast beef joint along the grain, and the slices are stringy and chewy. What should she have done?
o: Roasted it for a longer time at a lower heat
Carved it across the grain, with a sharp knife
Carved it while it was still very hot from the oven
Cut thicker slices, so the fibres hold together
questions.why: Cutting across the grain shortens the muscle fibres, so each slice is easier to chew. Cutting along them leaves long, tough strands.

questions.q: A guest develops a flushed face, a headache and a rash shortly after eating well-cooked tuna that spent hours in a warm van. What is the most likely cause?
o: Histamine that formed as the fish warmed, which cooking does not destroy
Salmonella from the fish, which should have been killed by cooking
An allergy to the oil in which the tuna was fried
Too much salt in the seasoning, which flushes the skin
questions.why: Fish such as tuna and mackerel make histamine if they get warm, and cooking does not remove it. Keep such fish cold from the boat to the pan, and buy from a trusted supplier.
